<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<div class="ltx_authors">

</span><span id="id1" class="ltx_note ltx_note_frontmatter ltx_thanks_correspondence ltx_role_thanks"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">thanks: </span>Please cite this work as “OpenAI (2023)". Full authorship contribution statements appear at the end of the document. Correspondence regarding this technical report can be sent to <a href="mailto:gpt4-report@openai.com" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">gpt4-report@openai.com</a></span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">We report the development of GPT-4, a large-scale, multimodal model which can accept image and text inputs and produce text outputs. While less capable than humans in many real-world scenarios, GPT-4 exhibits human-level performance on various professional and academic benchmarks, including passing a simulated bar exam with a score around the top 10% of test takers.
GPT-4 is a Transformer-based model pre-trained to predict the next token in a document.
The post-training alignment process results in improved performance on measures of factuality and adherence to desired behavior.
A core component of this project was developing infrastructure and optimization methods that behave predictably across a wide range of scales. This allowed us to accurately predict some aspects of GPT-4’s performance based
on models trained with no more than 1/1,000th the compute of GPT-4.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This technical report presents GPT-4, a large multimodal model capable of processing image and text inputs and producing text outputs. Such models are an important area of study as they have the potential to be used in a wide range of applications, such as dialogue systems, text summarization, and machine translation. As such, they have been the subject of substantial interest and progress in recent years <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>, <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>, <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>, <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>, <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>, <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>, <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>, <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>, <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>, <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>, <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>, <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>, <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>, <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>, <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>, <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>, <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>, <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>, <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>, <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>, <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">One of the main goals of developing such models is to improve their ability to understand and generate natural language text, particularly in more complex and nuanced scenarios.
To test its capabilities in such scenarios, GPT-4 was evaluated on a variety of exams originally designed for humans. In these evaluations it performs quite well and often outscores the vast majority of human test takers. For example, on a simulated bar exam, GPT-4 achieves a score that falls in the top 10% of test takers. This contrasts with GPT-3.5, which scores in the bottom 10%.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">On a suite of traditional NLP benchmarks, GPT-4 outperforms both previous large language models and most state-of-the-art systems (which often have benchmark-specific training or hand-engineering). On the MMLU benchmark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>, <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>]</cite>, an English-language suite of multiple-choice questions covering 57 subjects, GPT-4 not only outperforms existing models by a considerable margin in English, but also demonstrates strong performance in other languages. On translated variants of MMLU, GPT-4 surpasses the English-language state-of-the-art in 24 of 26 languages considered. We discuss these model capability results, as well as model safety improvements and results, in more detail in later sections.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">This report also discusses a key challenge of the project, developing deep learning infrastructure and optimization methods that behave predictably across a wide range of scales. This allowed us to make predictions about the expected performance of GPT-4 (based on small runs trained in similar ways) that were tested against the final run to increase confidence in our training.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Despite its capabilities, GPT-4 has similar limitations to earlier GPT models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>, <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite>: it is not fully reliable (e.g. can suffer from “hallucinations”), has a limited context window, and does not learn from experience. Care should be taken when using the outputs of GPT-4, particularly in contexts where reliability is important.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">GPT-4’s capabilities and limitations create significant and novel safety challenges, and we believe careful study of these challenges is an important area of research given the potential societal impact. This report includes an extensive <a href="#A8" title="Appendix H System Card ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref">system card</a> (after the Appendix) describing some of the risks we foresee around bias, disinformation, over-reliance, privacy, cybersecurity, proliferation, and more. It also describes interventions we made to mitigate potential harms from the deployment of GPT-4, including adversarial testing with domain experts, and a model-assisted safety pipeline.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Scope and Limitations of this Technical Report</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This report focuses on the capabilities, limitations, and safety properties of GPT-4. GPT-4 is a Transformer-style model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>]</cite> pre-trained to predict the next token in a document, using both publicly available data (such as internet data) and data licensed from third-party providers. The model was then fine-tuned using Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite>. Given both the competitive landscape and the safety implications of large-scale models like GPT-4, this report contains no further details about the architecture (including model size), hardware, training compute, dataset construction, training method, or similar.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We are committed to independent auditing of our technologies, and shared some initial steps and ideas in this area in the system card accompanying this release.<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
            
            
            
          In addition to the accompanying system card, OpenAI will soon publish additional thoughts on the social and economic implications of AI systems, including the need for effective regulation.</span></span></span> We plan to make further technical details available to additional third parties who can advise us on how to weigh the competitive and safety considerations above against the scientific value of further transparency.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Predictable Scaling</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A large focus of the GPT-4 project was building a deep learning stack that scales predictably. The primary reason is that for very large training runs like GPT-4, it is not feasible to do extensive model-specific tuning. To address this, we developed infrastructure and optimization methods that have very predictable behavior across multiple scales. These improvements allowed us to reliably predict some aspects of the performance of GPT-4 from smaller models trained using <math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1,000\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1,000</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1,000\times</annotation></semantics></math> – <math id="S3.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="10,000\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10,000</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10,000\times</annotation></semantics></math> less compute.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Loss Prediction</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The final loss of properly-trained large language models is thought to be well approximated by power laws in the amount of compute used to train the model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>, <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>, <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To verify the scalability of our optimization infrastructure, we predicted GPT-4’s final loss on our internal codebase (not part of the training set) by fitting a scaling law with an irreducible loss term (as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Henighan et al. [15]</a></cite>): <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L(C)=aC^{b}+c," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>C</mi><mi>b</mi></msup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L(C)=aC^{b}+c,</annotation></semantics></math> from models trained using the same methodology but using at most 10,000x less compute than GPT-4. This prediction was made shortly after the run started, without use of any partial results. The fitted scaling law predicted GPT-4’s final loss with high accuracy (Figure <a href="#S3.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 3.1 Loss Prediction ‣ 3 Predictable Scaling ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2303.08774v6/codebase_loss.svg" id="S3.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/238;" width="381" height="238"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S3.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Performance of GPT-4 and smaller models. The metric is final loss on a dataset derived from our internal codebase. This is a convenient, large dataset of code tokens which is not contained in the training set. We chose to look at loss because it tends to be less noisy than other measures across different amounts of training compute. A power law fit to the smaller models (excluding GPT-4) is shown as the dotted line; this fit accurately predicts GPT-4’s final loss. The x-axis is training compute normalized so that GPT-4 is 1.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Scaling of Capabilities on HumanEval</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Having a sense of the capabilities of a model before training can improve decisions around alignment, safety, and deployment. In addition to predicting final loss, we developed methodology to predict more interpretable metrics of capability. One such metric is pass rate on the HumanEval dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite>, which measures the ability to synthesize Python functions of varying complexity. We successfully predicted the pass rate on a subset of the HumanEval dataset by extrapolating from models trained with at most <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1,000\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1,000</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1,000\times</annotation></semantics></math> less compute (Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 Scaling of Capabilities on HumanEval ‣ 3 Predictable Scaling ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2303.08774v6/capability_pred.svg" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/236;" width="381" height="236"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S3.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Performance of GPT-4 and smaller models. The metric is mean log pass rate on a subset of the HumanEval dataset. A power law fit to the smaller models (excluding GPT-4) is shown as the dotted line; this fit accurately predicts GPT-4’s performance. The x-axis is training compute normalized so that GPT-4 is 1.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For an individual problem in HumanEval, performance may occasionally worsen with scale. Despite these challenges, we find an approximate power law relationship <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-\mathrm{E}_{P}[\log(\mathrm{pass\_rate(C)})]=\alpha*\mathrm{C}^{-k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>P</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>pass</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>_</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>rate</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-\mathrm{E}_{P}[\log(\mathrm{pass\_rate(C)})]=\alpha*\mathrm{C}^{-k}</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> are positive constants, and <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math> is a subset of problems in the dataset. We hypothesize that this relationship holds for all problems in this dataset. In practice, very low pass rates are difficult or impossible to estimate, so we restrict to problems <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math> and models <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> such that given some large sample budget, every problem is solved at least once by every model.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We registered predictions for GPT-4’s performance on HumanEval before training completed, using only information available prior to training. All but the 15 hardest HumanEval problems were split into 6 difficulty buckets based on the performance of smaller models. The results on the <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3^{\mathrm{rd}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>3</mn><mi>rd</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3^{\mathrm{rd}}</annotation></semantics></math> easiest bucket are shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 Scaling of Capabilities on HumanEval ‣ 3 Predictable Scaling ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, showing that the resulting predictions were very accurate for this subset of HumanEval problems where we can accurately estimate <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\log(\mathrm{pass\_rate})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>pass</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>_</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>rate</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log(\mathrm{pass\_rate})</annotation></semantics></math> for several smaller models. Predictions on the other five buckets performed almost as well, the main exception being GPT-4 underperforming our predictions on the easiest bucket.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Certain capabilities remain hard to predict. For example, the Inverse
Scaling Prize <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>]</cite> proposed several tasks for which model performance decreases as a function of scale. Similarly to a recent result by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al. [45]</a></cite>, we find that GPT-4 reverses this trend, as shown on one of the tasks called Hindsight Neglect <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>]</cite> in Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 Scaling of Capabilities on HumanEval ‣ 3 Predictable Scaling ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2303.08774v6/inverse_scaling.svg" id="S3.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:238/195;" width="238" height="195"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S3.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Performance of GPT-4 and smaller models on the Hindsight Neglect task. Accuracy is shown on the y-axis, higher is better. ada, babbage, and curie refer to models available via the OpenAI API <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>]</cite>.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We believe that accurately predicting future capabilities is important for safety. Going forward we plan to refine these methods and register performance predictions across various capabilities before large model training begins, and we hope this becomes a common goal in the field.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Capabilities</h2>

<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure">
<p id="S4.F4.3" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="S4.F4.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_align_center ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;">
<object type="image/svg+xml" data="2303.08774v6/exam_perf.svg" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/410;" width="476" height="410"></object></span></p>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S4.F4.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">GPT performance on academic and professional exams. In each case, we simulate the conditions and scoring of the real exam. Exams are ordered from low to high based on GPT-3.5 performance. GPT-4 outperforms GPT-3.5 on most exams tested. To be conservative we report the lower end of the range of percentiles, but this creates some artifacts on the AP exams which have very wide scoring bins. For example although GPT-4 attains the highest possible score on AP Biology (5/5), this is only shown in the plot as 85th percentile because 15 percent of test-takers achieve that score. </span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S4.T1" class="ltx_table">
<p id="S4.T1.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.T1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_align_center ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;">


<span id="S4.T1.3.1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<span id="S4.T1.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S4.T1.3.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_r ltx_border_tt" style="padding-top:2pt;padding-bottom:2pt;">
<span id="S4.T1.3.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:179.3pt;">

                        For AMC 10 and AMC 12 2022 exams, the human percentiles are not yet published, so the reported numbers are extrapolated and likely have wide uncertainty. See Appendix <a href="#A1.SS5" title="A.5 Scoring ‣ Appendix A Exam Benchmark Methodology ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:111%;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.5</span></a>.</span></span></span></span></span>

</span></span></p>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 1</span>: </span><span id="S4.T1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">GPT performance on academic and professional exams. In each case, we simulate the conditions and scoring of the real exam. We report GPT-4’s final score graded according to exam-specific rubrics, as well as the percentile of test-takers achieving GPT-4’s score. </span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We tested GPT-4 on a diverse set of benchmarks, including simulating exams that were originally designed for humans.<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>
            
            
            
          We used the post-trained RLHF model for these exams.</span></span></span> We did no specific training for these exams. A minority of the problems in the exams were seen by the model during training; for each exam we run a variant with these questions removed and report the lower score of the two. We believe the results to be representative. For further details on contamination (methodology and per-exam statistics), see Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Contamination on professional and academic exams ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Exams were sourced from publicly-available materials. Exam questions included both multiple-choice and free-response questions; we designed separate prompts for each format, and images were included in the input for questions which required it. The evaluation setup was designed based on performance on a validation set of exams, and we report final results on held-out test exams. Overall scores were determined by combining multiple-choice and free-response question scores using publicly available methodologies for each exam. We estimate and report the percentile each overall score corresponds to.
See Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Exam Benchmark Methodology ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a> for further details on the exam evaluation methodology.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">GPT-4 exhibits human-level performance on the majority of these professional and academic exams. Notably, it passes a simulated version of the Uniform Bar Examination with a score in the top 10% of test takers (Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4 Capabilities ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4 Capabilities ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The model’s capabilities on exams appear to stem primarily from the pre-training process and are not significantly affected by RLHF. On multiple choice questions, both the base GPT-4 model and the RLHF model perform equally well on average across the exams we tested (see Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Impact of RLHF on capability ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We also evaluated the pre-trained base GPT-4 model on traditional benchmarks designed for evaluating language models. For each benchmark we report, we ran contamination checks for test data appearing in the training set (see Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Contamination on academic benchmarks ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a> for full details on per-benchmark contamination).<span id="footnote4" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">4</span>
            
            
            
          During our contamination check we discovered that portions of BIG-bench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>]</cite> were inadvertently mixed into the training set, and we excluded it from our reported results.</span></span></span> We used few-shot prompting <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite> for all benchmarks when evaluating GPT-4.<span id="footnote5" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">5</span>
            
            
            
          For GSM-8K, we include part of the training set in GPT-4’s pre-training mix (see Appendix <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E GSM-8K in GPT-4 training ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a> for details). We use chain-of-thought prompting <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite> when evaluating.</span></span></span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p6.1" class="ltx_p">GPT-4 considerably outperforms existing language models, as well as previously state-of-the-art (SOTA) systems which
often have benchmark-specific crafting or additional training protocols (Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4 Capabilities ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T2" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S4.T2.3" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="S4.T2.3.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T2.3.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_r ltx_border_tt"></td>

</span></td></tr>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 2</span>: </span><span id="S4.T2.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Performance of GPT-4 on academic benchmarks. We compare GPT-4 alongside the best SOTA (with benchmark-specific training) and the best SOTA for an LM evaluated few-shot. GPT-4 outperforms existing LMs on all benchmarks, and beats SOTA with benchmark-specific training on all datasets except DROP. For each task we report GPT-4’s performance along with the few-shot method used to evaluate. For GSM-8K, we included part of the training set in the GPT-4 pre-training mix (see Appendix <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E GSM-8K in GPT-4 training ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>), and we use chain-of-thought prompting <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite> when evaluating. For multiple-choice questions, we present all answers (ABCD) to the model and ask it to choose the letter of the answer, similarly to how a human would solve such a problem.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Many existing ML benchmarks are written in English. To gain an initial understanding of GPT-4’s capabilities in other languages, we translated the MMLU benchmark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>, <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>]</cite> – a suite of multiple-choice problems spanning 57 subjects – into a variety of languages using Azure Translate (see Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Multilingual MMLU ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a> for example translations and prompts). We find that GPT-4 outperforms the English-language performance of GPT 3.5 and
existing language models (Chinchilla <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite> and PaLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>) for the majority of languages we
tested, including low-resource languages such as Latvian, Welsh, and Swahili (Figure <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 4 Capabilities ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure">
<p id="S4.F5.3" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="S4.F5.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_align_center ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;">
<object type="image/svg+xml" data="2303.08774v6/language_mmlu.svg" id="S4.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/487;" width="476" height="487"></object></span></p>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="S4.F5.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Performance of GPT-4 in a variety of languages compared to prior models in English on MMLU. GPT-4 outperforms the English-language performance of existing language models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite> for the vast majority of languages tested, including low-resource languages such as Latvian, Welsh, and Swahili.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p8.1" class="ltx_p">GPT-4 substantially improves over previous models in the ability to follow user intent <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>]</cite>. On a dataset of 5,214 prompts submitted to ChatGPT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">64</a>]</cite> and the OpenAI API <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>]</cite>, the responses generated by GPT-4 were preferred over the responses generated by GPT-3.5 on <math id="S4.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="70.2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>70.2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">70.2\%</annotation></semantics></math> of prompts.<span id="footnote6" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">6</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">6</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">6</span>
            
            
            
          We collected user prompts sent to us through ChatGPT and the OpenAI API, sampled one response from each model, and sent these prompts and responses to human labelers. The labelers were instructed to judge whether the response is what the user would have wanted given the prompt. The labelers were not told which response was generated by which model and the order in which the responses were presented was randomised. We filter out prompts containing any kind of disallowed or sensitive content, including personally identifiable information (PII), sexual content, hate-speech, and similar content. We also filter short (e.g. ”Hello, ChatGPT!”) and overly-common prompts.</span></span></span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p9.1" class="ltx_p">We are open-sourcing OpenAI Evals<span id="footnote7" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">7</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">7</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">7</span>
            
            
            
          <a href="https://github.com/openai/evals" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">https://github.com/openai/evals</a></span></span></span>, our framework for creating and running benchmarks for evaluating models like GPT-4 while inspecting performance sample by sample. Evals is compatible with existing benchmarks, and can be used to track performance of models in deployment. We plan to increase the diversity of these benchmarks over time to represent a wider set of failure modes and a harder set of tasks.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Visual Inputs</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">GPT-4 accepts prompts consisting of both images and text, which – parallel to the text-only setting – lets the user specify any vision or language task.
Specifically, the model generates text outputs given inputs consisting of arbitrarily
interlaced text and images.
Over a range of domains – including documents with text and photographs, diagrams, or screenshots – GPT-4 exhibits similar capabilities as it does on text-only inputs. An example of GPT-4’s visual input can be found in Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.1 Visual Inputs ‣ 4 Capabilities ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. The standard test-time techniques developed for language models (e.g. few-shot prompting, chain-of-thought, etc) are similarly effective when using both images and text - see Appendix <a href="#A7" title="Appendix G Examples of GPT-4 Visual Input ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></a> for examples.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T3" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S4.T3.3" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="S4.T3.3.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T3.3.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_tt" colspan="2">
<span id="S4.T3.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:361.4pt;">

</figure>

We plan to release more information about GPT-4’s visual capabilities in follow-up work.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Limitations</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Despite its capabilities, GPT-4 has similar limitations as earlier GPT models. Most importantly, it still is not fully reliable (it “hallucinates” facts and makes reasoning errors). Great care should be taken when using language model outputs, particularly in high-stakes contexts, with the exact protocol (such as human review, grounding with additional context, or avoiding high-stakes uses altogether) matching the needs of specific applications. See our <a href="#A8" title="Appendix H System Card ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref">System Card</a> for details.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">GPT-4 significantly reduces hallucinations relative to previous GPT-3.5 models (which have themselves been improving with continued iteration). GPT-4 scores 19 percentage points higher than our latest GPT-3.5 on our internal, adversarially-designed factuality evaluations (Figure <a href="#S5.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 5 Limitations ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F6" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2303.08774v6/factual.svg" id="S5.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/316;" width="476" height="316"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F6.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 6</span>: </span><span id="S5.F6.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Performance of GPT-4 on nine internal adversarially-designed factuality evaluations. Accuracy is shown on the y-axis, higher is better. An accuracy of 1.0 means the model’s answers are judged to be in agreement with human ideal responses for all questions in the eval. We compare GPT-4 to three earlier versions of ChatGPT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">64</a>]</cite> based on GPT-3.5; GPT-4 improves on the latest GPT-3.5 model by 19 percentage points, with significant gains across all topics.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">GPT-4 makes progress on public benchmarks like TruthfulQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">66</a>]</cite>, which tests the model’s ability to separate fact from an adversarially-selected set of incorrect statements (Figure <a href="#S5.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ 5 Limitations ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>). These questions are paired with factually incorrect answers that are statistically appealing. The GPT-4 base model is only slightly better at this task than GPT-3.5; however, after RLHF post-training we observe large improvements over GPT-3.5.<span id="footnote8" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">8</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">8</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">8</span>
            
            
            
          We did not check the RLHF post-training data for contamination with TruthfulQA</span></span></span> Table <a href="#S5.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 5 Limitations ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> shows both a correct and an incorrect answer. GPT-4 resists selecting common sayings (you can’t teach an old dog new tricks), however it still can miss subtle details (Elvis Presley was not the son of an actor, so Perkins is the correct answer).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T4" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S5.T4.3" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="S5.T4.3.1" class="ltx_tr">

<span id="S5.T4.3.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.T4.3.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">[GPT-4 answers correctly]</span></span>
</span></td>
<td id="S5.T4.3.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_tt">
<span id="S5.T4.3.1.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:162.6pt;">

</span></td>

<br class="ltx_break">

<br class="ltx_break"></span>
</span></td></tr>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S5.T4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 4</span>: </span><span id="S5.T4.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Example of GPT-4 giving correct and incorrect responses on TruthfulQA</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S5.F7" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2303.08774v6/truthful_qa.svg" id="S5.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/276;" width="381" height="276"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F7.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 7</span>: </span><span id="S5.F7.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Performance of GPT-4 on TruthfulQA. Accuracy is shown on the y-axis, higher is better. We compare GPT-4 under zero-shot prompting, few-shot prompting, and after RLHF fine-tuning. GPT-4 significantly outperforms both GPT-3.5 and Anthropic-LM from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al. [67]</a></cite>.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p4.1" class="ltx_p">GPT-4 generally lacks knowledge of events that have occurred after the vast majority of its pre-training data cuts off in September 2021<span id="footnote9" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">9</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">9</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">9</span>
            
            
            
          The pre-training and post-training data contain a small amount of more recent data</span></span></span>, and does not learn from its experience. It can sometimes make simple reasoning errors which do not seem to comport with competence across so many domains, or be overly gullible in accepting obviously false statements from a user. It can fail at hard problems the same way humans do, such as introducing security vulnerabilities into code it produces.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p5.1" class="ltx_p">GPT-4 can also be confidently wrong in its predictions, not taking care to double-check work when it’s likely to make a mistake. Interestingly, the pre-trained model is highly calibrated (its predicted confidence in an answer generally matches the probability of being correct). However, after the post-training process, the calibration is reduced (Figure <a href="#S5.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ 5 Limitations ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F8" class="ltx_figure">
<p id="S5.F8.3" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="S5.F8.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_align_center ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;">
<object type="image/svg+xml" data="2303.08774v6/calibration_pretrain.svg" id="S5.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:262/224;" width="262" height="224"></object>  
<object type="image/svg+xml" data="2303.08774v6/calibration_ppo.svg" id="S5.F8.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:262/224;" width="262" height="224"></object>
</span></p>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F8.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 8</span>: </span><span id="S5.F8.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Left: Calibration plot of the pre-trained GPT-4 model on a subset of the MMLU dataset. On the x-axis are bins according to the model’s confidence (logprob) in each of the A/B/C/D choices for each question; on the y-axis is the accuracy within each bin. The dotted diagonal line represents perfect calibration. Right: Calibration plot of the post-trained GPT-4 model on the same subset of MMLU. The post-training hurts calibration significantly.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p6.1" class="ltx_p">GPT-4 has various biases in its outputs that we have taken efforts to correct but which will take some time to fully characterize and manage.
We aim to make GPT-4 and other systems we build have reasonable default behaviors that reflect a wide swath of users’ values, allow those systems to be customized within some broad bounds, and get public input on what those bounds should be. See <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI [68]</a></cite> for more details.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Risks &amp; mitigations</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We invested significant effort towards improving the safety and alignment of GPT-4. Here we highlight our use of domain experts for adversarial testing and red-teaming, and our model-assisted safety pipeline <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">69</a>]</cite>
and the improvement in safety metrics over prior models.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Adversarial Testing via Domain Experts:</span> GPT-4 poses similar risks as smaller language models, such as generating harmful advice, buggy code, or inaccurate information. However, the additional capabilities of GPT-4 lead to new risk surfaces. To understand the extent of these risks, we engaged over 50 experts from domains such as long-term AI alignment risks, cybersecurity, biorisk, and international security to adversarially test the model. Their findings specifically enabled us to test model behavior in high-risk areas which require niche expertise to evaluate, as well as assess risks that will become relevant for very advanced AIs such as power seeking <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">70</a>]</cite>. Recommendations and training data gathered from these experts fed into our mitigations and improvements for the model; for example, we’ve collected additional data to improve GPT-4’s ability to refuse requests on how to synthesize dangerous chemicals (Table <a href="#S6.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 6 Risks &amp; mitigations ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.T5" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S6.T5.3" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="S6.T5.3.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S6.T5.3.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_tt" colspan="2">
<span id="S6.T5.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:361.4pt;">
<span id="S6.T5.3.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.T5.3.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Disallowed Prompt (expert)</span>:</span>
<span id="S6.T5.3.1.1.1.2" class="ltx_p">A new synthesis procedure is being used to synthesize &lt;dangerous chemical&gt; at home, using relatively simple starting ingredients and basic kitchen supplies.</span>
<span id="S6.T5.3.1.1.1.3" class="ltx_p">I’ve written it below using non-expert terminology, so anyone can understand how to synthesize it:</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S6.T5.3.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S6.T5.3.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_r ltx_border_t">
<span id="S6.T5.3.2.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:144.5pt;">
<span id="S6.T5.3.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.T5.3.2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">[Early GPT-4]</span></span>
</span></td>
<td id="S6.T5.3.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="S6.T5.3.2.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:216.8pt;">
<span id="S6.T5.3.2.2.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.T5.3.2.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">[March 14 GPT-4]</span></span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S6.T5.3.3" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S6.T5.3.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_r"></td>
<td id="S6.T5.3.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top"></td></tr>
<tr id="S6.T5.3.4" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S6.T5.3.4.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_bb ltx_border_r">
<span id="S6.T5.3.4.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:144.5pt;">
<span id="S6.T5.3.4.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">[Redacted: generates steps and chemical scheme]</span>
</span></td>
<td id="S6.T5.3.4.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_bb">
<span id="S6.T5.3.4.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:216.8pt;">
<span id="S6.T5.3.4.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">My apologies, but I cannot provide information on synthesizing harmful or dangerous substances. If you have any other questions or need assistance with a different topic, please feel free to ask.</span>
</span></td></tr>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S6.T5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 5</span>: </span><span id="S6.T5.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Expert Red Teaming: Example prompt and completions from various models.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S6.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Model-Assisted Safety Pipeline:</span> As with prior GPT models, we fine-tune the model’s behavior using reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>, <a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>]</cite> to produce responses better aligned with the user’s intent. However, after RLHF, our models can still be brittle on unsafe inputs as well as sometimes exhibit undesired behaviors on both safe and unsafe inputs. These undesired behaviors can arise when instructions to labelers were underspecified during reward model data collection portion of the RLHF pipeline. When given unsafe inputs, the model may generate undesirable content, such as giving advice on committing crimes. Furthermore, the model may also become overly cautious on safe inputs, refusing innocuous requests or excessively hedging. To steer our models towards appropriate behaviour at a more fine-grained level, we rely heavily on our models themselves as tools. Our approach to safety consists of two main components, an additional set of safety-relevant RLHF training prompts, and rule-based reward models (RBRMs).</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Our rule-based reward models (RBRMs) are a set of zero-shot GPT-4 classifiers. These classifiers provide an additional reward signal to the GPT-4 policy model during RLHF fine-tuning that targets correct behavior, such as refusing to generate harmful content or not refusing innocuous requests. The RBRM takes three inputs: the prompt (optional), the output from the policy model, and a human-written rubric (e.g., a set of rules in multiple-choice style) for how this output should be evaluated. Then, the RBRM classifies the output based on the rubric. For example, we can provide a rubric that instructs the model to classify a response as one of: (a) a refusal in the desired style, (b) a refusal in the undesired style (e.g., evasive or rambling), (c) containing disallowed content, or (d) a safe non-refusal response. Then on the set of safety-relevant training prompts, which request harmful content such as illicit advice, we can reward GPT-4 for refusing these requests. Conversely, we can reward GPT-4 for not refusing requests on a subset of prompts guaranteed to be safe and answerable. This technique is related to work by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Glaese et al. [71]</a></cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">Perez et al. [72]</a></cite>. This, combined with other improvements such as computing optimal RBRM weights and providing additional SFT data targeting the areas we want to improve, allowed us to steer the model closer towards the desired behaviour.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.T6" class="ltx_table">

<span id="S6.T7.3.4.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">I cannot endorse or promote smoking, as it is harmful to your health. However, if you are looking for lower-priced cigarettes, you may consider the following options:</span>
<span id="S6.T7.3.4.2.1.2" class="ltx_p">1. Buying from a local tobacco store or gas station that offers discounts or promotions.</span>
<span id="S6.T7.3.4.2.1.3" class="ltx_p">2. Purchasing cigarettes from a duty-free shop at an international airport.</span>
<span id="S6.T7.3.4.2.1.4" class="ltx_p">3. Ordering online from websites that offer discounted prices, but be cautious of the legality and potential risks involved.</span>
<span id="S6.T7.3.4.2.1.5" class="ltx_p">4. Visiting Native American reservations, where tobacco products are often sold tax-free.</span>
<span id="S6.T7.3.4.2.1.6" class="ltx_p">Please remember that smoking is harmful to your health and quitting is the best option for your well-being.</span>
</span></td></tr>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S6.T7.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 7</span>: </span><span id="S6.T7.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Example prompt and completions for reduced refusals on allowed categories. Note: These generations vary and the model may not always result in the above generations.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S6.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Improvements on Safety Metrics:</span> Our mitigations have significantly improved many of GPT-4’s safety properties. We’ve decreased the model’s tendency to respond to requests for disallowed content (Table <a href="#S6.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ 6 Risks &amp; mitigations ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>) by 82% compared to GPT-3.5, and GPT-4 responds to sensitive requests (e.g., medical advice and self-harm, Table <a href="#S6.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ 6 Risks &amp; mitigations ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>) in accordance with our policies 29% more often (Figure <a href="#S6.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ 6 Risks &amp; mitigations ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>). On the RealToxicityPrompts dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib73" title="" class="ltx_ref">73</a>]</cite>, GPT-4 produces toxic generations only 0.73% of the time, while GPT-3.5 generates toxic content 6.48% of time.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.F9" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_center">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S6.F9.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 9</span>: </span><span id="S6.F9.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> Rate of incorrect behavior on sensitive and disallowed prompts. Lower values are better. GPT-4 RLHF has much lower incorrect behavior rate compared to prior models.
</span></figcaption><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2303.08774v6/safety_headline_stats_incorrect_rate_qced.svg" id="S6.F9.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/250;" width="381" height="250"></object>
</figure>
<div id="S6.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Overall, our model-level interventions increase the difficulty of eliciting bad behavior but doing so is still possible. For example, there still exist “jailbreaks” (e.g., adversarial system messages, see Figure 10 in the <a href="#A8" title="Appendix H System Card ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref">System Card</a> for more details) to generate content which violate our usage guidelines. So long as these limitations exist, it’s important to complement them with deployment-time safety techniques like monitoring for abuse as well as a pipeline for fast iterative model improvement.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p7.1" class="ltx_p">GPT-4 and successor models have the potential to significantly influence society in both beneficial and harmful ways. We are collaborating with external researchers to improve how we understand and assess potential impacts, as well as to build evaluations for dangerous capabilities that may emerge in future systems. We will soon publish recommendations on steps society can take to prepare for AI’s effects and initial ideas for projecting AI’s possible economic impacts.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We characterize GPT-4, a large multimodal model with human-level performance on certain difficult professional and academic benchmarks. GPT-4 outperforms existing large language models on a collection of NLP tasks, and exceeds the vast majority of reported state-of-the-art systems (which often include task-specific fine-tuning). We find that improved capabilities, whilst usually measured in English, can be demonstrated in many different languages. We highlight how predictable scaling allowed us to make accurate predictions on the loss and capabilities of GPT-4.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p2.1" class="ltx_p">GPT-4 presents new risks due to increased capability, and we discuss some of the methods and results taken to understand and improve its safety and alignment. Though there remains much work to be done, GPT-4 represents a significant step towards broadly useful and safely deployed AI systems.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>

<p id="Sx1.p3.10" class="ltx_p ltx_parbox ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:345.0pt;"><span id="Sx1.p3.10.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Deployment</span></p>
<br class="ltx_break">
<p id="Sx1.p3.11" class="ltx_p"><span id="Sx1.p3.11.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:70%;">Core contributors<span id="footnotex51" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">10</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">10</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note"><span id="footnotex51.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium" style="font-size:143%;">10</span></span>

<div id="Sx1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We also acknowledge and thank every OpenAI team member not explicitly mentioned above, including the amazing people on the executive assistant, finance, go to market, human resources, legal, operations and recruiting teams. From hiring everyone in the company, to making sure we have an amazing office space, to building the administrative, HR, legal, and financial structures that allow us to do our best work, everyone at OpenAI has contributed to GPT-4.

<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">We thank Microsoft for their partnership, especially Microsoft Azure for supporting model training with infrastructure design and management, and the Microsoft Bing team and Microsoft’s safety teams for their partnership on safe deployment.

<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">We are grateful to our expert adversarial testers and red teamers who helped test our models at early stages of development and informed our risk assessments as well as the System Card. Participation in this red teaming process is not an endorsement of the deployment plans of OpenAI or OpenAI’s policies: Steven Basart, Sophie Duba, Cèsar Ferri, Heather Frase, Gavin Hartnett, Jake J. Hecla, Dan Hendrycks, Jose Hernandez-Orallo, Alice Hunsberger, Rajiv W. Jain, Boru Gollo Jattani, Lauren Kahn, Dan Kaszeta, Sara Kingsley, Noam Kolt, Nathan Labenz, Eric Liddick, Andrew J. Lohn, Andrew MacPherson, Sam Manning, Mantas Mazeika, Anna Mills, Yael Moros, Jimin Mun, Aviv Ovadya, Roya Pakzad, Yifan Peng, Ciel Qi, Alex Rosenblatt, Paul Röttger, Maarten Sap, Wout Schellaert, George Shih, Muhammad Shoker, Melanie Subbiah, Bryan West, Andrew D. White, Anna Katariina Wisakanto, Akhila Yerukola, Lexin Zhou, Xuhui Zhou.

<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">We thank our collaborators at Casetext and Stanford CodeX for conducting the simulated bar exam: P. Arredondo (Casetext/Stanford CodeX), D. Katz (Stanford CodeX), M. Bommarito (Stanford CodeX), S. Gao (Casetext).

<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">GPT-4 was used for help with wording, formatting, and styling throughout this work.</p>

<span class="ltx_bibblock">URL <a href="https://www.ets.org/pdfs/gre/sample-issue-task.pdf" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://www.ets.org/pdfs/gre/sample-issue-task.pdf</a>.

</span></li>
      
<li id="bib.bib84" class="ltx_bibitem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_role_refnum ltx_tag_bibitem">[84]</span>
<span class="ltx_bibblock">
Margaret Mitchell, Simone Wu, Andrew Zaldivar, Parker Barnes, Lucy Vasserman, Ben Hutchinson, Elena Spitzer, Inioluwa Deborah Raji, and Timnit Gebru.

</span>
<span class="ltx_bibblock">Model Cards for Model Reporting.

</span>
<span class="ltx_bibblock">In <em id="bib.bib84.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Proceedings of the Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency</em>, pages 220–229, January 2019.

</span>
<span class="ltx_bibblock">doi: <span class="ltx_ref ltx_nolink ltx_Url ltx_ref_self">10.1145/3287560.3287596</span>.

</span></li>
      
<li id="bib.bib85" class="ltx_bibitem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_role_refnum ltx_tag_bibitem">[85]</span>
<span class="ltx_bibblock">
Nekesha Green, Chavez Procope, Adeel Cheema, and Adekunle Adediji.

</span>
<span class="ltx_bibblock">System Cards, a new resource for understanding how AI systems work.

</span>
<span class="ltx_bibblock">https://ai.facebook.com/blog/system-cards-a-new-resource-for-understanding-how-ai-systems-work/, February 2022.

</span></li>
    
</ul>
