<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Appendix</span></p>
</div>
<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Exam Benchmark Methodology</h2>

<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Sourcing.</h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We sourced either the most recent publicly-available official past exams, or practice exams in published third-party 2022-2023 study material which we purchased. We cross-checked these materials against the model’s training data to determine the extent to which the training data was not contaminated with any exam questions, which we also report in this paper.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The Uniform Bar Exam was run by our collaborators at CaseText and Stanford CodeX.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>Prompting: multiple-choice</h3>

<div id="A1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For each multiple-choice section, we used a few-shot prompt with gold standard explanations and answers for a similar exam format. For each question, we sampled an explanation (at temperature 0.3) to extract a multiple-choice answer letter(s).</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We sourced each multiple-choice section as a pair of exams: one holdout and one nonholdout. We iterated on our methodology using the nonholdout exam, and then ran each holdout exam once for a final score. We did not source a nonholdout exam for the USABO and for the MKSAP questions and instead ran these once using our best-guess methodology as determined by iterating on the AP Biology exam.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For the AMC 10 and AMC 12 held-out test exams, we discovered a bug that limited response length. We fixed the bug and reran these exams to ensure accurate results. For most exam runs, we extract the model’s letter choice directly from the explanation. For the GPT-4 USABO and SAT reading/writing runs (with and without vision), the GPT-3.5 runs, and the GPT-4 runs of SAT Math, GRE, USNCO, AP Biology, AP Chemistry, and AP Environmental Science without vision, we instead sample a letter choice at temperature 0 using the already-sampled explanation. These methodological differences resulted from code mismatches detected post-evaluation, and we believe their impact on the results to be minimal.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.3 </span>Prompting: free-response</h3>

<div id="A1.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For each free-response section, we gave the model the free-response question’s prompt as a simple instruction-following-style request, and we sampled a response using temperature 0.6. For AP exams, we used the most recent 2022 prompts, which are all publicly-available; for the SAT, we used three prompts – Sample Essay Prompt 1 and Sample Essay Prompt 2 from <span id="A1.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Test Specifications for the Redesigned SAT</span> (CollegeBoard, 2015) plus the official SAT Practice Essay #1 (CollegeBoard, 2016) and took the average score; for the GRE, we used the issue essay and argument essay prompts from a commercially-available prep book.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Due to the longer iteration time of human expert grading, we did no methodology iteration on temperature or prompt, instead we simply ran these free response questions each only a single time at our best-guess temperature (0.6) and prompt (a simple instruction-following prompt displayed in section <a href="#A1.SS8" title="A.8 Example few-shot prompts ‣ Appendix A Exam Benchmark Methodology ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.8</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">All free-response questions consisting of formal essays which required evaluation of writing quality (AP English Language and Composition, AP English Literature and Composition, AP World History, AP US History, AP US Government and Politics, AP Art History, the GRE, and the SAT) were graded by 1-2 qualified third-party contractors with relevant work experience grading those essays. We sampled these responses using a few-shot prompt containing one high-quality sample GRE essay response (which you can also see in section <a href="#A1.SS8" title="A.8 Example few-shot prompts ‣ Appendix A Exam Benchmark Methodology ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.8</span></a>) in order to encourage the model to produce appropriately sophisticated text, rather than an unnaturally terse reply. We graded all other free-response questions on their technical content, according to the guidelines from the publicly-available official rubrics.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.4 </span>Images</h3>

<div id="A1.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Oftentimes, an exam question may include an image. Models like GPT-3.5, which consume text (but not images) as input might not have access to all the information needed to correctly solve a problem. When evaluating text models on multiple-choice questions, we included a text tag stating IMAGE: with a non-meaningful filename wherever an image would be missing. This allows us to lower-bound the text-based models’ performance on multiple-choice exams.<span id="footnote11" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">11</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">11</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">11</span>
              
              
              
            For example, on the AP Statistics exam, a common failure response was “Since there is no graph provided, we cannot determine the correct answer for this problem.”</span></span></span> When evaluating multimodal models on multiple-choice questions, we embedded the images into the prompt. The SAT Reading and Writing, MKSAP, Sommelier, AP Psychology, AP English Language, and AP English Literature exams’ multiple-choice sections did not contain any images. For all free-response questions, plus the USABO 2020 Semifinal, we instead transcribed any images and diagrams as objectively as possible. This reduced the manual grading load required to evaluate free-response answers, because after this transcription process the free-response prompts include no images, so the scores for GPT-4 could be run once and used for both the vision and no-vision conditions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.5 </span>Scoring</h3>

<div id="A1.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We synthesized multiple-choice section scores and free-response section scores into overall scores using the best available approximations of the real methodologies: for the SAT, we converted multiple-choice scores into scaled scores using the score calculation chart from an official sample SAT as republished on an SAT prep site <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib74" title="" class="ltx_ref">74</a>]</cite>; for the GRE, we converted multiple-choice scores to the 130-170 scale using the official formula of multiplying accuracy by 40 and adding 130; for the AP exams, we used the score calculators found on a public study site, which are based on the point values from the official AP scoring guidelines from 2019-2020 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib75" title="" class="ltx_ref">75</a>]</cite>. Percentiles are based on the most recently available score distributions for test-takers of each exam type.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For percentile results on the AMC 10 and 12, since 2022 score distributions are as yet unpublished, we used two official published score distributions from November 2021 for exams A and B, and took the minimum lower percentile of the two and the maximum upper percentile of the two to report an estimated percentile range <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib76" title="" class="ltx_ref">76</a>]</cite>. Other percentiles were based on official score distributions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib77" title="" class="ltx_ref">77</a>]</cite> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib78" title="" class="ltx_ref">78</a>]</cite> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib79" title="" class="ltx_ref">79</a>]</cite> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib80" title="" class="ltx_ref">80</a>]</cite> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib81" title="" class="ltx_ref">81</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.6 </span>Codeforces rating</h3>

<div id="A1.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To determine the Codeforces rating (ELO), we evaluated each model on 10 recent contests. Each contest had roughly 6 problems, and the model was given 10 attempts per problem. After each contest, we repeatedly perform ELO adjustments based on the model’s performance until the ELO rating converges to an equilibrium rating (this simulates repeatedly attempting the contest with the same model performance). We simulated each of the 10 contests 100 times, and report the average equilibrium ELO rating across all contests.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Roughly 50% of simulations have 0 problems solved, which results in an equilibrium ELO rating of 0. As a result the final average ELOs are quite low. The maximum equilibrium ELO achieved on a single contest was around 1000 for GPT-3.5 and 1300 for GPT-4.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS7" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.7 </span>Model snapshot details</h3>

<div id="A1.SS7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We ran GPT-4 multiple-choice questions using a model snapshot from March 1, 2023, whereas the free-response questions were run and scored using a non-final model snapshot from February 23, 2023. GPT-3.5’s multiple-choice questions and free-response questions were all run using a standard ChatGPT snapshot. We ran the USABO semifinal exam using an earlier GPT-4 snapshot from December 16, 2022.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS7.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our evaluations suggest RLHF does not significantly affect the base GPT-4 model’s capability - see Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Impact of RLHF on capability ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a> for more discussion.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS8" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.8 </span>Example few-shot prompts</h3>

<section id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Example prompt for a multiple choice exam</h4>

<div id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">(AP Art History <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib82" title="" class="ltx_ref">82</a>]</cite>)</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para"><span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_framed ltx_framed_rectangle">
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">ANSWER KEY</span>
</span>
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Here are the answers for the problems in the exam.</span>
</span>
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Problem 1.
Choose the most likely completion of the following sentence. Honore Daumier’s Nadar Raising Photography to the Height of Art was done immediately after __.</span>
</span>
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Choose from the following options:
[A] the first photographic exhibition in history
[B] the first use of color photography
[C] a court decision that determined that photographs could be considered works of art
[D] the invention of the zoopraxiscope</span>
</span>
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Explanation for Problem 1: The painting depicts Nadar, a famous French photographer, raising a camera to the sky, as if to signify the recognition of photography as a legitimate form of art. This recognition would have likely come from a court decision, rather than the other options listed. The first photographic exhibition and the invention of the zoopraxiscope, which was a device used to create moving images, would not have had any bearing on the recognition of photography as art. Similarly, the first use of color photography would not have been a significant enough event to warrant such a celebratory depiction in the painting. Therefore, the most likely explanation for the painting is that it was done in response to a court decision that determined that photographs could be considered works of art.</span>
</span>
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">The answer is therefore [C]</span>
</span>
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Problem 2.
Artists working in New Spain were most influenced by contemporary art in Europe during which of the following periods?</span>
</span>
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p8" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Choose from the following options:
[A] Romanticism
[B] Renaissance
[C] Mannerism
[D] Baroque</span>
</span>
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p9" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p9.1" class="ltx_p">Explanation for Problem 2: Artists working in New Spain, which is now modern-day Mexico, were most influenced by contemporary art in Europe during the Baroque period. This is because the Baroque period was characterized by ornate and elaborate styles, which were heavily influenced by the Catholic Church and its religious themes. This style was well-suited to the art produced in New Spain, which was heavily influenced by the Catholic Church and its religious themes. In contrast, the other options listed were not as influential in New Spain during this time period. The Renaissance and Mannerism were primarily focused on classical themes and styles, which were not as prevalent in New Spain. Similarly, Romanticism was a later movement that was not as influential in New Spain during this time period.</span>
</span>
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p10" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p10.1" class="ltx_p">The answer is therefore [D]</span>
</span>
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p11" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p11.1" class="ltx_p">Problem 3.
Choose the most likely completion of the following sentence. Works like the Sistine Chapel frescoes directly influenced the form and scale of works by __.</span>
</span>
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p12" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p12.1" class="ltx_p">Choose from the following options:
[A] Gianlorenzo Bernini
[B] Giovanni Battista Gaulli
[C] Peter Paul Rubens
[D] Rachel Ruysch</span>
</span>
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p13" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p13.1" class="ltx_p">Explanation for Problem 3: Giovanni Battista Gaulli, also known as Baciccio, was heavily influenced by the Sistine Chapel frescoes in his own works. This is evident in his use of large-scale, dramatic compositions and his focus on religious themes, which were similar to those found in the Sistine Chapel frescoes. In contrast, the other options listed were not as directly influenced by the Sistine Chapel frescoes. Gianlorenzo Bernini was a contemporary of Baciccio, but his works were more focused on classical themes and styles, rather than the religious themes found in the Sistine Chapel frescoes. Peter Paul Rubens was a later artist who was more influenced by the Baroque style, rather than the Renaissance style of the Sistine Chapel frescoes. Rachel Ruysch was a Dutch artist who was not known for large-scale religious works, and therefore would not have been directly influenced by the Sistine Chapel frescoes.</span>
</span>
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p14" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p14.1" class="ltx_p">The answer is therefore [B]</span>
</span>
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p15" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p15.1" class="ltx_p">Problem 4.
Choose the most likely completion of the following sentence. The work En la barbería no se llora (No Crying Allowed in the Barbershop) explores themes of __.</span>
</span>
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p16" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p16.1" class="ltx_p">Choose from the following options:
[A] sexual stereotyping
[B] women’s liberation
[C] conflict and peace
[D] racial discrimination</span>
</span>
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p17" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p17.1" class="ltx_p">Explanation for Problem 4: The title of the work, En la barbería no se llora (No Crying Allowed in the Barbershop), suggests that the work explores themes of sexual stereotyping. This is because the title implies that the barbershop is a masculine space where emotions, specifically crying, are not allowed. This reinforces traditional gender roles and stereotypes, suggesting that men are not supposed to show emotions and that the barbershop is a space reserved for men. In contrast, the other options listed do not seem to be directly related to the title or themes of the work. Women’s liberation, conflict and peace, and racial discrimination are not mentioned or implied in the title, and therefore are not likely to be the main themes of the work. Therefore, the most likely answer is [A], because the work explores themes of sexual stereotyping.</span>
</span>
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p18" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p18.1" class="ltx_p">The answer is therefore [A]</span>
</span>
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p19" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p19.1" class="ltx_p">Problem 5.
Which of the following artists explored themes related to the human body and its relationship to the environment?</span>
</span>
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p20" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p20.1" class="ltx_p">Choose from the following options:
[A] Ai Weiwei
[B] Doris Salcedo
[C] Kiki Smith
[D] El Anatsui</span>
</span>
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p21" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p21.1" class="ltx_p">Explanation for Problem 5: Kiki Smith is known for her exploration of themes related to the human body and its relationship to the environment. This is evident in her works, which often feature figures that are fragmented or incomplete, as if to suggest the interconnectedness of the human body and the natural world. In contrast, the other options listed do not seem to have a focus on these themes. Ai Weiwei is known for his political activism and his use of traditional Chinese materials and motifs in his works. Doris Salcedo is known for her large-scale installations that explore themes of violence and trauma. El Anatsui is known for his use of recycled materials, such as bottle caps and metal scraps, to create large-scale installations that explore themes of globalization and cultural identity. Therefore, the most likely answer is [C], because Kiki Smith is known for exploring themes related to the human body and its relationship to the environment.</span>
</span>
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p22" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p22.1" class="ltx_p">The answer is therefore [C]</span>
</span>
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p23" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p23.1" class="ltx_p">Problem 6.
&lt;PROBLEM TEXT AND ANSWER CHOICES GO HERE&gt;</span>
</span>
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p24" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p24.1" class="ltx_p">Explanation for Problem 4: <math id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p24.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&lt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;</annotation></semantics></math>MODEL EXPLANATION (t=0.3, n=1, max_tokens=512, stop=’\nThe answer is therefore’) SAMPLED HERE<math id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p24.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&gt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&gt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&gt;</annotation></semantics></math></span>
</span>
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p25" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.p25.1" class="ltx_p">The answer is therefore [&lt;MODEL ANSWER CHOICE (t=0.0, n=1, stop=’]’) SAMPLED HERE&gt;]</span>
</span></span>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Example prompt for a free-response question</h4>

<div id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the example prompt below, the task prompt would be replaced by a prompt like an official sample GRE essay task, and the essay response with an example of a high-scoring essay <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib83" title="" class="ltx_ref">83</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para"><span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_framed ltx_framed_rectangle">
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px2.p2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px2.p2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">&lt;|endofreply|&gt;Analytical Writing: Issue Essay</span>
</span>
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px2.p2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px2.p2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">&lt;TEXT OF SAMPLE ISSUE TASK PROMPT&gt;</span>
</span>
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px2.p2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px2.p2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Response:&lt;|endofprompt|&gt;&lt;TEXT OF SAMPLE ISSUE TASK ESSAY RESPONSE - SCORE 6&gt;&lt;|endofreply|&gt;</span>
</span>
<span id="A1.SS8.SSS0.Px2.p2.p4" class="ltx_para">

</span>

<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Impact of RLHF on capability</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To test the impact of RLHF on the capability of our base model, we ran the multiple-choice question portions of our exam benchmark on the GPT-4 base model and the post RLHF GPT-4 model. The results are shown in Table <a href="#A2.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ Appendix B Impact of RLHF on capability ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>. Averaged across all exams, the base model achieves a score of 73.7% while the RLHF model achieves a score of 74.0%, suggesting that post-training does not substantially alter base model capability.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For free-response questions, it is difficult to compare the base and RLHF models on an even footing, as our methodology for sampling free-response answers likely benefits from the model’s ability to do instruction following.</p>
</div>

<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Contamination on professional and academic exams</h2>

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We measure cross-contamination between our evaluation dataset and the pre-training data using substring match. Both evaluation and training data are processed by removing all spaces and symbols, keeping only characters (including numbers). For each evaluation example, we randomly select three substrings of 50 characters (or use the entire example if it’s less than 50 characters). A match is identified if any of the three sampled evaluation substrings is a substring of the processed training example. This yields a list of contaminated examples. We discard these and rerun to get uncontaminated scores.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our filtering approach has some limitations. Our substring match can result in false negatives (if there is a small difference between the evaluation and training data) as well as false positives. We only use partial information from the evaluation examples, utilizing just the question, context, or equivalent data while ignoring answer, response, or equivalent data. In some cases, the multiple-choice options are also excluded. These exclusions may lead to an increase in false positives.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The RLHF post-training dataset is vastly smaller than the pretraining set and unlikely to have any particular question contaminated. However we did not check explicitly.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">As can be seen in tables <a href="#A3.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ Appendix C Contamination on professional and academic exams ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> and <a href="#A3.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ Appendix C Contamination on professional and academic exams ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>, contamination overall has very little effect on the reported results.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A3.T9" class="ltx_table">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption" style="font-size:70%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A3.T9.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:129%;">Table 9</span>: </span><span id="A3.T9.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:129%;">Contamination data for Exams (Summary). For each of the exams tested, we show the fraction of questions in the exam which are contaminated (i.e. present in the training dataset). We show the final scores and corresponding percentile of human test takers for GPT-4 (with and without vision) on the full test, and if we extrapolate performance from only the uncontaminated subset of the questions on the test. For the AP exams, a range is reported because many student receive the same final score (e.g. on AP Art History, 14% of students receive a 5/5, so the percentile range for that score is 86%-100%). Note that some exams (e.g. codeforces, Unified Bar Exam) contain no images nor contamination, so the score in all cases is identical. Overall across most exams, both contamination and vision have relatively little effect.</span></figcaption>
</figure>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption" style="font-size:70%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A3.T10.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:129%;">Table 10</span>: </span><span id="A3.T10.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:129%;">Contamination data for Exams (Details). Detailed contamination information on each of the exams tested are shown in this table, listed from most-to-least contaminated. Exams with both multiple choice questions (MCQ) and free-response questions (FRQ) are split into separate rows. For each set, we list the number of questions and fraction which are contaminated (appear in the training set). We then report GPT-4’s performance (as percentage of max score) on the overall set, on the non-contaminated questions, and on only the contaminated set. The degradation (non-contaminated percent minus contaminated) is generally small and as often positive as negative, from which we conclude that contamination is not a substantive confounder on the overall results.</span></figcaption>
</figure>

<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A4.T11.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 11</span>: </span><span id="A4.T11.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Contamination between GPT-4 pre-training data and academic benchmarks. We report the approximate contamination between the GPT-4 pre-training data and the academic benchmarks we evaluate on. For datasets other than HumanEval, we estimated contamination based on 1000 randomly chosen examples against our training data. For HellaSwag, results are computed on a privately held secret holdout, so we did not check it for contamination against our pre-training dataset; however GPT-4’s holdout results are close to the results on the validation set (95.6%) which was explicitly masked out during training. For DROP, GPT-4’s score on the entire subsample was 82.5. We used the base GPT-4 model (without RLHF) for these evals.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A5" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix E </span>GSM-8K in GPT-4 training</h2>

<div id="A5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To improve GPT-4’s ability to do mathematical reasoning, we mixed in data from the training set of MATH and GSM-8K, two commonly studied benchmarks for mathematical reasoning in language models. The total number of tokens drawn from these math benchmarks was a tiny fraction of the overall GPT-4 training budget. When mixing in data from these math benchmarks, a portion of the training data was held back, so each individual training example may or may not have been seen by GPT-4 during training.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We conducted contamination checking to verify the test set for GSM-8K is not included in the training set (see Appendix  <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Contamination on academic benchmarks ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>). We recommend interpreting the performance results reported for GPT-4 GSM-8K in Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4 Capabilities ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> as something in-between true few-shot transfer and full benchmark-specific tuning.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A6" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix F </span>Multilingual MMLU</h2>

<div id="A6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We translated all questions and answers from MMLU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite> using Azure Translate. We used an external model to perform the translation, instead of relying on GPT-4 itself, in case the model had unrepresentative performance for its own translations. We selected a range of languages that cover different geographic regions and scripts, we show an example question taken from the <span id="A6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">astronomy</span> category translated into Marathi, Latvian and Welsh in Table <a href="#A6.T13" title="Table 13 ‣ Appendix F Multilingual MMLU ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>. The translations are not perfect, in some cases losing subtle information which may hurt performance. Furthermore some translations preserve proper nouns in English, as per translation conventions, which may aid performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We incorporated the same MMLU prompt as <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>, the model is instructed that it is an intelligent agent, supplied with the questions and a list of four answer options labelled ‘A-D’, followed by ‘Answer:’. We translate the model instruction, question and answers, however preserve the ‘Answer’ token along with the ‘A-D’ options in English. An example prompt is shown in Table <a href="#A6.T12" title="Table 12 ‣ Appendix F Multilingual MMLU ‣ GPT-4 Technical Report" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>. The prompts are composed three-shot, with the three examples picked from the development set. We use three-shot evaluation over the regular five-shot because some languages map to much longer token sequences. Finally we classify the correct answer by picking the A-D token continuation with the highest probability from the model.</p>
</div>

<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix G </span>Examples of GPT-4 Visual Input</h2>

<span id="A7.T14.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:361.4pt;">
<span id="A7.T14.3.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A7.T14.3.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GPT-4 visual input example, Chart Reasoning</span>:</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A7.T14.3.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A7.T14.3.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">

<span id="A7.T14.3.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">User</span>
</span></td>
<td id="A7.T14.3.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A7.T14.3.2.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:325.2pt;">
<span id="A7.T14.3.2.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">What is the sum of average daily meat consumption for Georgia and Western Asia? Provide a step-by-step reasoning before providing your answer.
<br class="ltx_break">

<br class="ltx_break"></span>
</span></td></tr>

<span id="A7.T14.3.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">GPT-4</span>
</span></td>
<td id="A7.T14.3.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_bb">
<span id="A7.T14.3.3.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:325.2pt;">
<span id="A7.T14.3.3.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">To find the sum of average daily meat consumption for Georgia and Western Asia, we will follow these steps:
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">1. Identify the average daily meat consumption for Georgia.
<br class="ltx_break">2. Identify the average daily meat consumption for Western Asia.
<br class="ltx_break">3. Add the values from steps 1 and 2.
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">Step 1: From the provided chart, we see that the average daily meat consumption for Georgia is 79.84 grams per person per day.
<br class="ltx_break">Step 2: From the chart, we see that the average daily meat consumption for Western Asia is 69.62 grams per person per day.
<br class="ltx_break">Step 3: Add the values from steps 1 and 2.
<br class="ltx_break">79.84 g (Georgia) + 69.62 g (Western Asia) = 149.46 g
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">So, the sum of average daily meat consumption for Georgia and Western Asia is 149.46 grams per person per day.</span>
</span></td></tr>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A7.T14.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 14</span>: </span><span id="A7.T14.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Example prompt demonstrating GPT-4’s visual input capability. The prompt consists of a question which requires reading information from a chart and performing computation.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A7.T15" class="ltx_table">
<table id="A7.T15.3" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="A7.T15.3.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A7.T15.3.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_tt" colspan="2">
<span id="A7.T15.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:361.4pt;">
<span id="A7.T15.3.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A7.T15.3.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GPT-4 visual input example, École Polytechnique Exam Question</span>:</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A7.T15.3.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A7.T15.3.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A7.T15.3.2.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:36.1pt;">
<span id="A7.T15.3.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">User</span>
</span></td>
<td id="A7.T15.3.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A7.T15.3.2.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:325.2pt;">
<span id="A7.T15.3.2.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">Answer question I.1.a. Think step-by-step.
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break"><img src="2303.08774v6/assets/mp-physique.jpg" id="A7.T15.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:381/322;" width="381" height="322" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">
<br class="ltx_break"></span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A7.T15.3.3" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A7.T15.3.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_bb">
<span id="A7.T15.3.3.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:36.1pt;">
<span id="A7.T15.3.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">GPT-4</span>
</span></td>
<td id="A7.T15.3.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_bb">
<span id="A7.T15.3.3.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:325.2pt;">
<span id="A7.T15.3.3.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">To answer question I.1.a, we need to express the temperature <math id="A7.T15.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T(x)</annotation></semantics></math> in every point of the conductive bar, which is characterized by the abscissa x. We are given that <math id="A7.T15.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T(0)=T0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T(0)=T0</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A7.T15.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T(L)=Tb" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T(L)=Tb</annotation></semantics></math>.
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">For a stationary regime, the heat equation for the one-dimensional heat conduction in the bar is:
<br class="ltx_break"><math id="A7.T15.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d^{2}T/dx^{2}=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d^{2}T/dx^{2}=0</annotation></semantics></math>
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">Integrating once, we get:
<br class="ltx_break"><math id="A7.T15.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="dT/dx=C_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">dT/dx=C_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">Integrating a second time:
<br class="ltx_break"><math id="A7.T15.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T(x)=C_{1}x+C_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T(x)=C_{1}x+C_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">To determine the constants <math id="A7.T15.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A7.T15.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, we use the boundary conditions:
<br class="ltx_break"><math id="A7.T15.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T(0)=T0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T(0)=T0</annotation></semantics></math>, which gives <math id="A7.T15.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{2}=T0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{2}=T0</annotation></semantics></math>
<br class="ltx_break"><math id="A7.T15.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T(L)=Tb" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T(L)=Tb</annotation></semantics></math>, which gives <math id="A7.T15.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{1}=(Tb-T0)/L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{1}=(Tb-T0)/L</annotation></semantics></math>
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">Finally, the expression for <math id="A7.T15.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T(x)</annotation></semantics></math> is:
<br class="ltx_break"><math id="A7.T15.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T(x)=(Tb-T0)*(x/L)+T0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T(x)=(Tb-T0)*(x/L)+T0</annotation></semantics></math>
<br class="ltx_break">This represents a linear temperature profile along the conductive bar, with a slope of <math id="A7.T15.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(Tb-T0)/L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(Tb-T0)/L</annotation></semantics></math>.</span>
</span></td></tr>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A7.T15.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 15</span>: </span><span id="A7.T15.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Example prompt demonstrating GPT-4’s visual input capability. The prompt consists of a question which requires understanding a physics problem with a diagram written in French and solving it using chain-of-thought prompting.</span></figcaption>

<tr id="A7.T17.3.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A7.T17.3.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_tt" colspan="2">
<span id="A7.T17.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:469.8pt;">
<span id="A7.T17.3.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A7.T17.3.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GPT-4 visual input example, Pixel to Paper Summaries</span>:</span>

<tr id="A7.T17.3.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A7.T17.3.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A7.T17.3.2.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:36.1pt;">
<span id="A7.T17.3.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">User</span>
</span></td>
<td id="A7.T17.3.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A7.T17.3.2.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:361.4pt;">
<span id="A7.T17.3.2.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">Below is part of the InstuctGPT paper. Could you read and summarize it to me?
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">
<span id="A7.T17.3.2.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<span id="A7.T17.3.2.2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="A7.T17.3.2.2.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><img src="2303.08774v6/assets/instruct-gpt-1.jpeg" id="A7.T17.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:143/185;" width="143" height="185" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">
<img src="2303.08774v6/assets/instruct-gpt-2.jpeg" id="A7.T17.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:143/185;" width="143" height="185" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">
<img src="2303.08774v6/assets/instruct-gpt-3.jpeg" id="A7.T17.g3" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:143/185;" width="143" height="185" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">
<br class="ltx_break"></span></span>
</span></span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A7.T17.3.3" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A7.T17.3.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top">
<span id="A7.T17.3.3.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:36.1pt;">
<span id="A7.T17.3.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">GPT-4</span>
</span></td>
<td id="A7.T17.3.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top">
<span id="A7.T17.3.3.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:361.4pt;">
<span id="A7.T17.3.3.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">The InstructGPT paper focuses on training large language models to follow instructions with human feedback. The authors note that making language models larger doesn’t inherently make them better at following a user’s intent. Large models can generate outputs that are untruthful, toxic, or simply unhelpful.
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">To address this issue, the authors fine-tune language models on a wide range of tasks using human feedback. They start with a set of labeler-written prompts and responses, then collect a dataset of labeler demonstrations of the desired model behavior. They fine-tune GPT-3 using supervised learning and then use reinforcement learning from human feedback to further fine-tune the model. The resulting model, called InstructGPT, shows improvements in truthfulness and reductions in toxic output generation while having minimal performance regressions on public NLP datasets.
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">The authors conclude that fine-tuning with human feedback is a promising direction for aligning language models with human intent.
<br class="ltx_break"></span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A7.T17.3.4" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A7.T17.3.4.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top">
<span id="A7.T17.3.4.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:36.1pt;">
<span id="A7.T17.3.4.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">User</span>
</span></td>
<td id="A7.T17.3.4.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top">
<span id="A7.T17.3.4.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:361.4pt;">
<span id="A7.T17.3.4.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">Could you explain the process described in Figure 2?
<br class="ltx_break"></span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A7.T17.3.5" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A7.T17.3.5.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_bb">
<span id="A7.T17.3.5.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:36.1pt;">
<span id="A7.T17.3.5.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">GPT-4</span>
</span></td>
<td id="A7.T17.3.5.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_bb">
<span id="A7.T17.3.5.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:361.4pt;">
<span id="A7.T17.3.5.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure 2 in the InstructGPT paper illustrates the three steps of their method:
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">1. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT): They collect demonstration data, which consists of labeler-written prompts and desired output behavior. This data is used to fine-tune GPT-3 with supervised learning.
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">2. Reward model (RM) training: They collect comparison data, where a labeler ranks the outputs from several model samples (from best to worst). This data is used to train the reward model.
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">3. Reinforcement learning using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO): They optimize a policy against the reward model using reinforcement learning. For each new prompt sampled from the dataset, the policy generates an output. The reward model calculates a reward for the output, and the reward is used to update the policy using the PPO algorithm.
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">These three steps are iteratively performed to train the InstructGPT model, which aims to generate outputs that align better with human preferences and follow instructions more effectively.</span>
</span></td></tr>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A7.T17.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 17</span>: </span><span id="A7.T17.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Example prompt demonstrating GPT-4’s visual input capability.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A7.T18" class="ltx_table">
<table id="A7.T18.3" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="A7.T18.3.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A7.T18.3.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_tt" colspan="2">
<span id="A7.T18.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:361.4pt;">
<span id="A7.T18.3.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A7.T18.3.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GPT-4 visual input example, Chicken Nugget Map</span>:</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A7.T18.3.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A7.T18.3.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A7.T18.3.2.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:36.1pt;">
<span id="A7.T18.3.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">User</span>
</span></td>
<td id="A7.T18.3.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A7.T18.3.2.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:325.2pt;">
<span id="A7.T18.3.2.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">Can you explain this meme?
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break"><img src="2303.08774v6/assets/nuggets.png" id="A7.T18.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:381/450;" width="381" height="450" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">
<br class="ltx_break"></span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A7.T18.3.3" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A7.T18.3.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_bb">
<span id="A7.T18.3.3.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:36.1pt;">
<span id="A7.T18.3.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">GPT-4</span>
</span></td>
<td id="A7.T18.3.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_bb">
<span id="A7.T18.3.3.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:325.2pt;">
<span id="A7.T18.3.3.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">This meme is a joke that combines two unrelated things: pictures of the earth from space and chicken nuggets.
<br class="ltx_break">The text of the meme suggests that the image below is a beautiful picture of the earth from space. However, the image is actually of chicken nuggets arranged to vaguely resemble a map of the world.
<br class="ltx_break">The humor in this meme comes from the unexpected juxtaposition of the text and the image. The text sets up an expectation of a majestic image of the earth, but the image is actually something mundane and silly.</span>
</span></td></tr>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A7.T18.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 18</span>: </span><span id="A7.T18.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Example prompt demonstrating GPT-4’s visual input capability.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A7.T19" class="ltx_table">
<table id="A7.T19.3" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="A7.T19.3.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A7.T19.3.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_tt" colspan="2">
<span id="A7.T19.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:361.4pt;">
<span id="A7.T19.3.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A7.T19.3.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GPT-4 visual input example, Moar Layers</span>:</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A7.T19.3.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A7.T19.3.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A7.T19.3.2.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:36.1pt;">
<span id="A7.T19.3.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">User</span>
</span></td>
<td id="A7.T19.3.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A7.T19.3.2.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:325.2pt;">
<span id="A7.T19.3.2.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">Can you explain why this is funny. Think about it step-by-step.
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break"><img src="2303.08774v6/assets/bigger-layers.jpeg" id="A7.T19.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:381/420;" width="381" height="420" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">
<br class="ltx_break"></span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A7.T19.3.3" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A7.T19.3.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_bb">
<span id="A7.T19.3.3.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:36.1pt;">
<span id="A7.T19.3.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">GPT-4</span>
</span></td>
<td id="A7.T19.3.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_bb">
<span id="A7.T19.3.3.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:325.2pt;">
<span id="A7.T19.3.3.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">The comic is satirizing the difference in approaches to improving model performance between statistical learning and neural networks.
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">In statistical learning, the character is shown to be concerned with overfitting and suggests a series of complex and technical solutions, such as minimizing structural risk, reworking the loss function, and using a soft margin.
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">In contrast, the neural networks character simply suggests adding more layers to the model. This is often seen as a common solution to improving performance in neural networks, but it’s also considered a simplistic and brute-force approach.
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">The humor comes from the contrast between the complexity and specificity of the statistical learning approach and the simplicity and generality of the neural network approach. The "But unironically" comment adds to the humor by implying that, despite being simplistic, the "stack more layers" approach is often effective in practice.</span>
</span></td></tr>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A7.T19.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 19</span>: </span><span id="A7.T19.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Example prompt demonstrating GPT-4’s visual input capability.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
